newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones stock skids on flat results, Telerate investment.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones stock skids on flat results, Telerate investment.

text.p: Dow Jones & Co. Inc. reported flat earnings for the fourth quarter and full year Monday and shocked Wall Street with plans to spend up to $650 million to revitalise and expand its Dow Jones Telerate financial information services unit.
The company's stock slid $4.125 to $36.75 on the New York Stock Exchange as investors were surprised by the scope of the three to four-year effort to turn around Telerate.

"We recognise we have slipped some in this business recently relative to our competitors," Chairman and Chief Executive Peter Kann told industry analysts in a conference call. "We intend to reverse that situation.
"Make no mistake. It will be a costly programme," Kann said.
Dow Jones competes with Reuters Holdings PLC and Bloomberg LP providing information in major financial markets.

Dow Jones, a diversified financial services and publishing company, reported fourth-quarter earnings of $59.6 million, or 62 cents a share, flat with year-ago profits of $59.9 million, or 62 cents a share. Revenues rose to $671 million from $612 million.

For the year, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal and Barron's earned $189.9 million, or $1.96 a share, on revenues of $2.48 billion. In 1995 it earned $189.6 million, or $1.96 a share, on revenues of $2.28 billion.

According to First Call, which monitors Wall Street earnings outlooks, the consensus for the latest quarter was 60 cents per a and $1.84 for the full year. For 1997, First Call has projected earnings of $1.94 a share.
The company estimated that after the Telerate costs, 1997 earnings will be between $1.20 and $1.40 a share, and said its 1998 results also will be affected by the programme.
"Wall Street is a little shocked at the expenditures to fix Telerate," said Oppenheimer & Co. analyst Edward Atorino.

Dow Jones' stock gained $3.125 to $38.875 last week after a Fortune magazine article detailed efforts among younger members of the family that controls the media company to push management to improve shareholder value.
"It went up for a strange reason," Attorino said.

Smith Barney analyst Steven Barlow said the market took "all (of the gain) back and rightfully so." He said analysts had been curious since October about what Dow Jones planned to do with Telerate and how much it would be willing to invest in the unit.
"I didn't think it would be this high a number," Barlow said.

The company's business publishing unit, which includes print publications, television operations and the Business Information Services group, posted a full-year revenue increase of 15.7 percent to just over $1.2 billion.
Revenues at Dow Jones' financial information services unit, which includes the Dow Jones Telerate and Financial News Services groups, advanced 1.9 percent to $979.7 million.
Ottaway Newspapers, Inc., the company's community newspaper subsidiary, reported a 5.4 percent revenue gain to $287.5 million.
